# gh-1087: [GOAL] Quota circuit-breaker: provider-quota exhaustion (403 usage-limit) parks the lane instead of per-tick retry burn (live: fa gh-1697 loop risk)

## Description

## Goal — provider-quota exhaustion parks the leg lane instead of per-tick retry burn (v1)

One sentence: **a hard provider-quota failure (403 weekly/usage-limit, not transient 429) parks the ticket's leg lane with a visible label and a reason comment** — retries resume only after the quota window resets or a human reconfigures the provider — instead of resetting the ticket for an immediate retry that is guaranteed to fail again.

Live: fa gh-1697, 2026-10-19 06:31–06:33Z — z.ai `glm-5.3-flash` answered 403 "weekly (7-day) usage limit" (9 retries), the whole provider chain exhausted, fa exited 1, gh-742 reset the ticket to Ready For Development. The next SM tick re-dispatches the same leg into the same exhausted chain — a burn loop measured in runner-minutes and noise comments until the 7-day window resets.

## Root cause

The interruption classifier treats a quota-exhausted chain the same as a transient interruption (rate limit blip, network cut). Transients deserve immediate retry; a 7-day quota wall does not. The signal is distinguishable: HTTP 403 with a usage-limit body vs 429 rate-limit.

## Acceptance criteria (testable)

- **AC1** — The leg's agent-failure classification distinguishes `quota_exhausted` (403 usage-limit / billing bodies, "Provider chain exhausted" after quota responses) from `transient` (429, timeouts, cuts). Fixture-driven unit test on the classifier.
- **AC2** — On `quota_exhausted`: the ticket is NOT reset to Ready For Development; instead it (and the PR if present) gets a park label (e.g. `provider_quota`) with a comment naming the provider, the quota window text, and the reset condition. The SM excludes the label from dispatch lanes.
- **AC3** — The park self-lifts when a bounded probe (one cheap provider ping per N ticks, not a full leg) succeeds — or a human removes the label. Probe cadence and the label name are config (`jobParams`), defaults sane.
- **AC4** — Transient interruptions keep today's gh-742 behavior exactly (reset + retry) — regression guard.

## Test plan

- `UT-1` — classifier: 403-weekly-limit → quota_exhausted; 429 → transient; mixed chain ending in quota → quota_exhausted (AC1).
- `UT-2` — park path: label + comment + no status reset (AC2); probe-success un-park (AC3).
- `REG-1` — gh-742 reset-path tests unchanged on transient fixtures (AC4).

## Non-goals

- Provider failover config (the chain already exists and was exhausted — this card governs the aftermath, not provider selection).
- Cross-repo quota accounting.

## References

- Live: fa gh-1697 dev leg, run 39210285663 (2026-10-19 06:33Z), "Provider chain exhausted: 2 of 2"
- gh-742 (interrupted-mid-run reset — correct for transients)

+# Quota Park Probe
+
+Bounded self-lift for the gh-1087 provider-quota park: runs locally on every SM tick against tickets carrying the park label (default `provider_quota`) and fires one cheap provider ping only when the recorded probe count hits the `jobParams.quotaProbeEveryNTicks` cadence (default 3 ticks).
+
+Probe success means the quota window has reset or the provider was reconfigured — the handler removes the park label, clears the development/rework dispatch trigger labels, moves the ticket back to Ready For Development and posts an un-park comment, so the normal dispatch lanes resume on the next tick. Probe failure keeps the park and posts a one-line `quota-probe: <n>` marker comment that doubles as the durable counter for the next tick's cadence decision.
+
+## Parameters
+
+- `jobParams.quotaParkLabel` — park label name to watch and remove (default `provider_quota`). When overridden, the SM rule's JQL (`labels = provider_quota`) must be overridden to match.
+- `jobParams.quotaProbeEveryNTicks` — probe cadence in SM ticks (default 3). The first tick after the park always probes (a misclassification self-corrects immediately).
+- `jobParams.quotaProbeCommand` — the cheap provider ping shell command (default: a 1-token chat completion against the fa provider config `FA_PROVIDER_BASE_URL` / `FA_PROVIDER_API_KEY` / `FA_PROVIDER_MODEL`; curl `--fail` keeps the park on any HTTP error). Override for non-fa provider shapes.
+
+A human un-parks immediately by removing the park label from the ticket — the probe rule stops matching and no further probes fire.

arguments.content:
🚨 **BLOCKING: Probe cadence deadlocks after the first failed probe — the park never self-lifts (AC3 broken)**

The cadence design has a counter-advance flaw. `probeDue(priorProbeCount, everyN)` fires only when `priorProbeCount % everyN === 0`, and `priorProbeCount` (`countProbeMarkers`) only advances when a probe actually fires and posts its `quota-probe: <n>` marker. Tracing the composed system (`quotaParkProbe.action`) with a provider that stays quota-blocked:

- Tick 1: no markers → count 0, `0 % 3 === 0` → probe #1 fires, marker `quota-probe: 1` posted.
- Tick 2+: count is **1**, `1 % 3 !== 0` → `probe_not_due`, no marker posted, count never advances.

Probe #2 can therefore never fire — 1 is never a multiple of 3 and nothing else moves the counter. Verified by direct simulation of the shipped pure functions over 12 successive SM ticks: exactly **one** probe fires, then silence until a human removes the label. For the live motivating case (a 7-day weekly quota wall) the park effectively never self-lifts, which defeats the ticket's AC3 ("The park self-lifts when a bounded probe (one cheap provider ping per N ticks) succeeds").

The unit tests miss this because `probeDue` is only tested in isolation and the `probe_not_due` test mocks `quota-probe: 1` directly — no test drives two successive failing ticks through `quotaParkProbe.action`.

The root cause is that an **attempts-only** counter cannot encode a **tick-based** cadence. Options:

1. Record every tick, not every probe — e.g. post a lightweight `quota-park-tick: n` marker each tick and probe when `n % everyN === 0` (noisy but correct).
2. Derive due-ness from the last probe marker comment's timestamp vs the SM tick interval (needs a tick-duration config).
3. Repurpose the counter as "probes since last decision" — fire when `(priorCount % everyN) === 0` counting **decision points**, which requires recording each decision point (same as option 1).

Whichever option is chosen, please also add an integration test that runs `quotaParkProbe.action` (or the composed loop) for at least `2 × everyN` consecutive failing ticks and asserts a second probe fires.

💡 **SUGGESTION: Log a redacted probe command**

```javascript
console.log('Running probe #' + probeCount + ':', command);
```

The full probe command is logged verbatim on every probe. The default command only references env-var *names* (`$FA_PROVIDER_API_KEY`), so the default is safe — but `jobParams.quotaProbeCommand` is a free-form shell string, and if an operator overrides it with an inline credential (e.g. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..."`), the key lands in the SM job logs and possibly CI artifacts. Consider logging a redacted form, e.g. the command with `-H` header values masked, or just the probe number and the override's presence.

Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ### External-spec evidence rule A finding whose core claim is "**the spec / reference / ticket / external tool says or does X**" may be raised at 🚨 **BLOCKING** only when it quotes the exact source the review actually read during this run — a `file:line` reference or a doc URL. A bare "the spec says …" assertion is unfalsifiable for the author and for the machine, and a false one holds a validated PR hostage (live: a BLOCKING thread claiming an exemption list that the reference source did not contain — the reviewed code was behaviorally identical to it). Without a verifiable citation: - Downgrade the finding to ⚠️ **IMPORTANT**, phrased as a question: "Please confirm against `` — if confirmed, this becomes blocking." - Never let an uncited spec assertion be the sole reason for `REQUEST_CHANGES`. This is not a strictness cut: a spec-claim finding **with** a verifiable citation keeps full 🚨 BLOCKING force. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. # gh-1087: [GOAL] Quota circuit-breaker: provider-quota exhaustion (403 usage-limit) parks the lane instead of per-tick retry burn (live: fa gh-1697 loop risk)

## Description

## Goal — provider-quota exhaustion parks the leg lane instead of per-tick retry burn (v1)

One sentence: **a hard provider-quota failure (403 weekly/usage-limit, not transient 429) parks the ticket's leg lane with a visible label and a reason comment** — retries resume only after the quota window resets or a human reconfigures the provider — instead of resetting the ticket for an immediate retry that is guaranteed to fail again.

Live: fa gh-1697, 2026-10-19 06:31–06:33Z — z.ai `glm-5.3-flash` answered 403 "weekly (7-day) usage limit" (9 retries), the whole provider chain exhausted, fa exited 1, gh-742 reset the ticket to Ready For Development. The next SM tick re-dispatches the same leg into the same exhausted chain — a burn loop measured in runner-minutes and noise comments until the 7-day window resets.

## Root cause

The interruption classifier treats a quota-exhausted chain the same as a transient interruption (rate limit blip, network cut). Transients deserve immediate retry; a 7-day quota wall does not. The signal is distinguishable: HTTP 403 with a usage-limit body vs 429 rate-limit.

## Acceptance criteria (testable)

- **AC1** — The leg's agent-failure classification distinguishes `quota_exhausted` (403 usage-limit / billing bodies, "Provider chain exhausted" after quota responses) from `transient` (429, timeouts, cuts). Fixture-driven unit test on the classifier.
- **AC2** — On `quota_exhausted`: the ticket is NOT reset to Ready For Development; instead it (and the PR if present) gets a park label (e.g. `provider_quota`) with a comment naming the provider, the quota window text, and the reset condition. The SM excludes the label from dispatch lanes.
- **AC3** — The park self-lifts when a bounded probe (one cheap provider ping per N ticks, not a full leg) succeeds — or a human removes the label. Probe cadence and the label name are config (`jobParams`), defaults sane.
- **AC4** — Transient interruptions keep today's gh-742 behavior exactly (reset + retry) — regression guard.

## Test plan

- `UT-1` — classifier: 403-weekly-limit → quota_exhausted; 429 → transient; mixed chain ending in quota → quota_exhausted (AC1).
- `UT-2` — park path: label + comment + no status reset (AC2); probe-success un-park (AC3).
- `REG-1` — gh-742 reset-path tests unchanged on transient fixtures (AC4).

## Non-goals

- Provider failover config (the chain already exists and was exhausted — this card governs the aftermath, not provider selection).
- Cross-repo quota accounting.

## References

- Live: fa gh-1697 dev leg, run 39210285663 (2026-10-19 06:33Z), "Provider chain exhausted: 2 of 2"
- gh-742 (interrupted-mid-run reset — correct for transients)

{"content":"🚨 **BLOCKING: Probe cadence deadlocks after the first failed probe — the park never self-lifts (AC3 broken)**

The cadence design has a counter-advance flaw. `probeDue(priorProbeCount, everyN)` fires only when `priorProbeCount % everyN === 0`, and `priorProbeCount` (`countProbeMarkers`) only advances when a probe actually fires and posts its `quota-probe: <n>` marker. Tracing the composed system (`quotaParkProbe.action`) with a provider that stays quota-blocked:

- Tick 1: no markers → count 0, `0 % 3 === 0` → probe #1 fires, marker `quota-probe: 1` posted.
- Tick 2+: count is **1**, `1 % 3 !== 0` → `probe_not_due`, no marker posted, count never advances.

Probe #2 can therefore never fire — 1 is never a multiple of 3 and nothing else moves the counter. Verified by direct simulation of the shipped pure functions over 12 successive SM ticks: exactly **one** probe fires, then silence until a human removes the label. For the live motivating case (a 7-day weekly quota wall) the park effectively never self-lifts, which defeats the ticket's AC3 ("The park self-lifts when a bounded probe (one cheap provider ping per N ticks) succeeds").

The unit tests miss this because `probeDue` is only tested in isolation and the `probe_not_due` test mocks `quota-probe: 1` directly — no test drives two successive failing ticks through `quotaParkProbe.action`.

The root cause is that an **attempts-only** counter cannot encode a **tick-based** cadence. Options:

1. Record every tick, not every probe — e.g. post a lightweight `quota-park-tick: n` marker each tick and probe when `n % everyN === 0` (noisy but correct).
2. Derive due-ness from the last probe marker comment's timestamp vs the SM tick interval (needs a tick-duration config).
3. Repurpose the counter as "probes since last decision" — fire when `(priorCount % everyN) === 0` counting **decision points**, which requires recording each decision point (same as option 1).

Whichever option is chosen, please also add an integration test that runs `quotaParkProbe.action` (or the composed loop) for at least `2 × everyN` consecutive failing ticks and asserts a second probe fires.

Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. This is not a strictness cut: a spec-claim finding **with** a verifiable citation keeps full 🚨 BLOCKING force. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. One sentence: **a hard provider-quota failure (403 weekly/usage-limit, not transient 429) parks the ticket's leg lane with a visible label and a reason comment** — retries resume only after the quota window resets or a human reconfigures the provider — instead of resetting the ticket for an immediate retry that is guaranteed to fail again.

Live: fa gh-1697, 2026-10-19 06:31–06:33Z — z.ai `glm-5.3-flash` answered 403 "weekly (7-day) usage limit" (9 retries), the whole provider chain exhausted, fa exited 1, gh-742 reset the ticket to Ready For Development. The next SM tick re-dispatches the same leg into the same exhausted chain — a burn loop measured in runner-minutes and noise comments until the 7-day window resets.

## Root cause

The interruption classifier treats a quota-exhausted chain the same as a transient interruption (rate limit blip, network cut). Transients deserve immediate retry; a 7-day quota wall does not. The signal is distinguishable: HTTP 403 with a usage-limit body vs 429 rate-limit.

## Acceptance criteria (testable)

- **AC1** — The leg's agent-failure classification distinguishes `quota_exhausted` (403 usage-limit / billing bodies, "Provider chain exhausted" after quota responses) from `transient` (429, timeouts, cuts). Fixture-driven unit test on the classifier.
- **AC2** — On `quota_exhausted`: the ticket is NOT reset to Ready For Development; instead it (and the PR if present) gets a park label (e.g. `provider_quota`) with a comment naming the provider, the quota window text, and the reset condition. The SM excludes the label from dispatch lanes.
- **AC3** — The park self-lifts when a bounded probe (one cheap provider ping per N ticks, not a full leg) succeeds — or a human removes the label. Probe cadence and the label name are config (`jobParams`), defaults sane.
- **AC4** — Transient interruptions keep today's gh-742 behavior exactly (reset + retry) — regression guard.

## Test plan

- `UT-1` — classifier: 403-weekly-limit → quota_exhausted; 429 → transient; mixed chain ending in quota → quota_exhausted (AC1).
- `UT-2` — park path: label + comment + no status reset (AC2); probe-success un-park (AC3).
- `REG-1` — gh-742 reset-path tests unchanged on transient fixtures (AC4).

## Non-goals

- Provider failover config (the chain already exists and was exhausted — this card governs the aftermath, not provider selection).
- Cross-repo quota accounting.

## References

- Live: fa gh-1697 dev leg, run 39210285663 (2026-10-19 06:33Z), "Provider chain exhausted: 2 of 2"
- gh-742 (interrupted-mid-run reset — correct for transients)

{"content":"🚨 **BLOCKING: Probe cadence deadlocks after the first failed probe — the park never self-lifts (AC3 broken)**

The cadence design has a counter-advance flaw. `probeDue(priorProbeCount, everyN)` fires only when `priorProbeCount % everyN === 0`, and `priorProbeCount` (`countProbeMarkers`) only advances when a probe actually fires and posts its `quota-probe: <n>` marker. Tracing the composed system (`quotaParkProbe.action`) with a provider that stays quota-blocked:

- Tick 1: no markers → count 0, `0 % 3 === 0` → probe #1 fires, marker `quota-probe: 1` posted.
- Tick 2+: count is **1**, `1 % 3 !== 0` → `probe_not_due`, no marker posted, count never advances.

Probe #2 can therefore never fire — 1 is never a multiple of 3 and nothing else moves the counter. Verified by direct simulation of the shipped pure functions over 12 successive SM ticks: exactly **one** probe fires, then silence until a human removes the label. For the live motivating case (a 7-day weekly quota wall) the park effectively never self-lifts, which defeats the ticket's AC3 ("The park self-lifts when a bounded probe (one cheap provider ping per N ticks) succeeds").

The unit tests miss this because `probeDue` is only tested in isolation and the `probe_not_due` test mocks `quota-probe: 1` directly — no test drives two successive failing ticks through `quotaParkProbe.action`.

The root cause is that an **attempts-only** counter cannot encode a **tick-based** cadence. Options:

1. Record every tick, not every probe — e.g. post a lightweight `quota-park-tick: n` marker each tick and probe when `n % everyN === 0` (noisy but correct).
2. Derive due-ness from the last probe marker comment's timestamp vs the SM tick interval (needs a tick-duration config).
3. Repurpose the counter as "probes since last decision" — fire when `(priorCount % everyN) === 0` counting **decision points**, which requires recording each decision point (same as option 1).

Whichever option is chosen, please also add an integration test that runs `quotaParkProbe.action` (or the composed loop) for at least `2 × everyN` consecutive failing ticks and asserts a second probe fires.
